analysis.summary:
This 68-year-old male presents with a 20-year history of chronic relapsing-remitting scaly red rash with itching, now acutely worsened over one week with progressive inflammatory signs (yellow exudate, crusting). The constellation of findings is entirely consistent with underlying Spleen Qi and Yang deficiency manifesting as chronic Damp-Heat accumulation in the skin, now escalated to acute Heat-Toxin complication. The tongue diagnosis—red body with thick yellow greasy coating—is pathognomonic for Damp-Heat (the red indicating Heat, the yellow coating indicating Heat within Dampness, the greasiness indicating trapped moisture). The pulse, slippery and rapid, corroborates this: the slippery quality reflects pathogenic dampness; the rapid rate confirms underlying Heat driving the pulse faster and forcing the fluids outward.

The patient's digestive dysfunction (sticky mouth, poor appetite, sticky/incomplete-evacuation stools) indicates Spleen and Stomach Qi failing to transform and transport water properly—the root mechanism by which dampness accumulates. The fatigue and heavy body sensation are classic Spleen-deficiency complaints aggravated by dampness obstructing Qi flow. The 20-year duration establishes this as a chronic constitutional pattern, not an acute external invasion; the acute worsening this week represents an exacerbation of the smoldering Damp-Heat into active Heat-Toxin, likely triggered by dietary excess, heat exposure, or stress.

The treatment strategy must address both the acute pathogenic excess (Damp-Heat and Heat-Toxin, which are 標/superficial manifestations) and the underlying Spleen deficiency (本/root cause). Clearing heat and draining dampness will resolve the immediate skin eruption and itching, while concurrently tonifying Spleen function will prevent recurrence. The patient's age (68) and chronicity mean that pure bitter-cold formulas risk further damaging Spleen Yang; thus herbs that simultaneously clear damp-heat AND tonify Spleen function are preferred (such as Job's tears, white atractylodes, and poria). Dietary modification is equally critical: the patient must eliminate foods that promote dampness (dairy, greasy foods, excess sweets) and favor bland easily-digested foods that support Spleen function while gently clearing damp-heat (winter melon, mung beans, barley, small fish).

analysis.pattern_rationale: The primary pattern of Spleen Qi and Yang Deficiency with Damp-Heat Accumulation and Heat Toxin is identified by integrating every data point: (1) Spleen Qi deficiency is evidenced by poor appetite, fatigue, heavy sensation, and sticky incomplete stools—all canonical Spleen-deficiency presentations; (2) Spleen Yang deficiency specifically is suggested by the sticky stools (Yang Qi failure to warm/move water) and the 20-year chronicity at age 68 (Yang naturally declines with age); (3) Damp-Heat is diagnosed from the red tongue with thick yellow greasy coating (the 'greasy' texture is the key sign of trapped moisture), the slippery-rapid pulse (classic Damp-Heat pulse), and the sticky mouth and stools (Damp-Heat blocking digestive Qi); (4) Heat-Toxin is demonstrated by the acute escalation with yellow exudate and crusting (exudate = pus = Heat-Toxin manifestation, not simple inflammation); (5) the chronicity (20 years) rules out acute exterior syndromes and identifies this as a Liver-Spleen constitutional weakness; (6) the itching is a sign of chronic Heat consuming Yin (Yin is the 'cooling lubricant', so Yin deficiency = increased Heat sensation on skin); (7) the sleep disturbance from itching indicates Shen (Spirit) disturbance from Heat. No competing pattern fits: this is neither pure Spleen deficiency (the acute heat signs are too prominent), nor pure Damp-Heat (the digestive weakness and fatigue are too entrenched for a simple 'pathogen' diagnosis). The 20-year history makes this a 虚实夹杂 (deficiency-excess complex), with the acute flare-up making the excess (Damp-Heat / Heat-Toxin) currently dominant, but the underlying Spleen deficiency driving the disease recurrence and chronicity.

treatment.therapeutic_principle: Clear Heat and Resolve Dampness to extinguish Heat-Toxin (priority 1); Tonify Spleen Qi and Yang to restore the root function of water transformation and prevent recurrence (priority 2); Harmonize and protect Spleen function so that bitter-cold heat-clearing herbs do not further damage digestion.
treatment.treatment_method: Use a modified Si Miao San (Four Marvel Powder) formula as the base, which is the classical TCM treatment for Damp-Heat conditions affecting the skin. Add white atractylodes (Bai Zhu) and poria (Fu Ling) to support Spleen water-transformation function concurrently. Supplement with heat-toxin resolving herbs such as honeysuckle flower (Jin Yin Hua) and forsythia fruit (Lian Qiao) to address the acute exudate and infection. Provide the formula as a decoction (simmered medicinal tea) taken warm twice daily. Simultaneously implement strict dietary therapy to remove dampness-promoting foods and favor bland easily-digested Spleen-supporting foods. Perform daily acupoint massage at Spleen points (SP9, ST36) and heat-clearing points (LI11) to supplement herbal treatment. Guide lifestyle changes to avoid humidity, heat, and emotional stress. Expect initial improvements (reduced itching, better sleep) within 1–2 weeks; visible skin healing within 4–8 weeks; and full constitutional strengthening over 3–6 months. Treat acutely until heat-toxin signs (exudate, crusting, severe inflammation) fully resolve, then transition to a Spleen-tonifying maintenance phase to prevent relapse.

beneficial: Job's Tears (薏米, Yi Yi Ren) — sweet, bland, cool; drains dampness while gently supporting Spleen, resolves heat-toxin; use in congee or soup 3–5 times per week
Winter Melon (冬瓜, Dong Gua) — sweet, cool, drains pathogenic water without damaging Spleen; promotes urination; eat steamed or in soup 2–3 times per week
Mung Beans (绿豆, Lü Dou) — sweet, cold; clear heat, drain dampness, resolve toxin; especially beneficial for skin conditions; make into congee or soup 2–3 times per week
Chinese Yam (山药, Shan Yao) — sweet, bland, warm; tonifies Spleen Yang and aids digestion while not aggravating dampness; steam or boil in congee 4–5 times per week
Pearl Barley (薏米) or Barley (大麦, Da Mai) — bitter, sweet, cool; drains dampness, aids digestion; cook as porridge or add to soups 3–4 times per week
recipes: Anti-Damp-Heat Congee: Cook 50g Job's tears (Yi Yi Ren) + 100g rice + 30g Chinese yam + 6 red dates (jujubes) in 1 liter water for 45 minutes until very soft. Add salt to taste. Eat warm for breakfast 3–4 times per week. Purpose: Tonifies Spleen, drains dampness, supports skin healing.

Clear-Heat Winter Melon Soup: Simmer 300g diced winter melon + 100g mung beans + 50g Job's tears + 6 cups water for 40 minutes. Add salt lightly. Drink warm. Can be eaten 2–3 times per week as a main dish component. Purpose: Drains damp-heat, cools the body, resolves heat-toxin from skin.

foods_to_avoid: Dairy products (milk, cheese, yogurt, ice cream) — sweet and creamy, they strengthen dampness accumulation and obstruct Spleen Qi transformation
Greasy and fried foods (fatty meat, pork belly, fried snacks, cooking oils in excess) — saturated fats aggravate dampness and heat-toxin, worsening skin eruptions
Sugary and sweet foods (desserts, candy, honey, sugary drinks, refined grains) — excess sweet flavor damages Spleen function and promotes dampness-heat fermentation
lifestyle: Avoid prolonged humidity and damp environments — sleep in a dry, well-ventilated bedroom; use air conditioning or dehumidifier if environment is humid; avoid basement living or working in wet conditions, as external dampness enters the body and aggravates internal damp-heat

Avoid excessive heat exposure — do not take hot baths (warm showers only), avoid saunas, avoid prolonged sun exposure in summer, do not overheat through excessive clothing; Heat aggravates skin condition and accelerates acute flare-ups

Maintain gentle movement and regular activity — take a 30-minute walk at moderate pace, 4–5 times per week; avoid strenuous exercise that causes excessive sweating (sweating damages fluids and Qi), but sedentary behavior stagnates Qi and aggravates dampness; find balance

Manage emotional stress through relaxation — practice meditation or tai chi 15–20 minutes daily; emotional worry and stress directly damage Spleen function and drive Liver Qi stagnation, perpetuating damp-heat; cultivate optimism and joy to support Spleen
acupoints: ST36 Zusanli (足三里) — Location: 3 cun below ST35 (Dubi, the depression below the kneecap), one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the bony ridge of the shinbone). Technique: Apply firm circular pressure with your thumb for 2–3 minutes, 1–2 times daily. Purpose: Tonifies Spleen Qi and Stomach function, improves digestion and appetite, strengthens overall Qi—critical for addressing the underlying deficiency.

SP9 Yinlingquan (阴陵泉) — Location: In the depression on the medial (inner) side of the knee, directly below the medial tibial condyle (inner knee bony bump), at the level where the knee crease ends. Technique: Apply firm circular pressure with your thumb for 2–3 minutes, 1–2 times daily. Purpose: Primary point for resolving pathogenic dampness, tonifies Spleen Yang, drains water retention—directly addresses the damp-heat pathogen.

LI11 Quchi (曲池) — Location: In the lateral (outer) end of the crease at the elbow, at the elbow fold when the arm is bent at 90 degrees. Technique: Apply firm to moderate pressure with your thumb for 1–2 minutes, 1–2 times daily. Purpose: Clears Heat and drains damp-heat, especially effective for skin manifestations on the arms and face—locally treats the heat component of the eruption.
exercise: Tai Chi (太極拳) or similar gentle flowing movement — practice 20–30 minutes, 3–4 times per week; tai chi moves Qi without causing excessive sweating, strengthens Spleen Yang, and calms the Shen (spirit), supporting both physical and emotional healing

Moderate-pace walking — walk at a steady pace (able to speak but not sing) for 30–45 minutes, 4–5 times per week; walking aids digestion, moves Qi to prevent stagnation, and gently strengthens Spleen function without overheating the body
recommendations.emotional_care: The 20-year history of chronic skin disease often generates emotional frustration, anxiety, and self-consciousness. Excessive worry and rumination directly damage Spleen function and perpetuate the disease cycle. Cultivate emotional resilience by: (1) practicing self-compassion—recognize that chronic illness is not a personal failure; (2) engaging in enjoyable activities (hobbies, socializing, nature exposure) to support Liver Qi flow and Spleen joy; (3) setting realistic expectations—improvements may take 8–12 weeks; (4) considering professional support (counseling or CBT) if anxiety or depression is prominent; (5) practicing daily meditation or mindfulness (10–15 minutes) to calm the Shen and reduce emotional stress. Emotional balance is as important as herbs and diet for breaking the damp-heat cycle.

herbal_formulas.name: Modified Si Miao San (四妙散) with Spleen Support and Heat-Toxin Clearing
ingredients: Cang Zhu (苍术, Atractylodes lancea) 10g — dries dampness, moves Qi, bitters Heat
Huang Bai (黄柏, Phellodendron amurense) 10g — bitter, cold; clears heat and drains damp-heat
Yi Yi Ren (薏米, Coix lacryma-jobi) 20g — sweet, bland; drains dampness AND tonifies Spleen Qi; resolves heat-toxin
Huai Niu Xi (怀牛膝, Achyranthes bidentata) 10g — guides heat downward, moves blood
Bai Zhu (白术, Atractylodes macrocephala) 10g — tonifies Spleen, aids water transformation (note: different species from Cang Zhu; this is the tonifying version)
Fu Ling (茯苓, Poria cocos) 15g — sweet, bland; aids water metabolism, tonifies Spleen, calms Shen
Jin Yin Hua (金银花, Lonicera japonica) 12g — sweet, cold; clears heat-toxin, especially effective for skin eruptions
Lian Qiao (连翘, Forsythia suspensa) 12g — bitter, cool; clears heat-toxin and resolves skin lesions
Bai Xian Pi (白鲜皮, Dictamnus dasycarpus) 12g — bitter, cold; treats itching and dermatosis, heat-toxin
Chen Pi (陈皮, Citrus reticulata aged peel) 6g — promotes digestion, moves Qi, prevents herbs from clogging digestion
Gan Cao (甘草, Glycyrrhiza uralensis) 6g — sweet; harmonizes all herbs, tonifies Qi, protects Spleen
herbal_formulas.dosage: Decoction (traditional simmered medicinal tea): 1 packet per day. Simmer for 45 minutes in 3 cups water until 1.5 cups liquid remains. Divide into 2 doses (morning and evening). Drink warm, preferably 30 minutes before meals. Continue for 2–3 weeks, then reassess with TCM practitioner. Do not extend beyond 4 weeks without professional review, as long-term cold herbs can injure Spleen Yang if Qi deficiency worsens.
herbal_formulas.purpose: Simultaneously clears Damp-Heat and Heat-Toxin (addressing the acute 標/manifestation), while tonifying Spleen Qi and Yang (addressing the chronic 本/root). The formula is specifically designed for 68-year-old patient with underlying deficiency—it avoids the over-cooling mistakes of pure heat-clearing formulas. Yi Yi Ren is the 'star' ingredient, combining heat-toxin resolution with Spleen support. The additions of Bai Zhu, Fu Ling, and Gan Cao ensure that digestion is protected rather than further damaged during treatment.

warning_signs: Rapidly spreading rash or new areas of eruption appearing within hours — may indicate systemic allergic reaction or serious infection
Fever (temperature ≥38.5°C / 101°F) accompanying skin lesions — suggests secondary bacterial infection or systemic heat-toxin; seek conventional medical evaluation immediately
Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, or purulent drainage from skin lesions — signs of worsening infection; may require antibiotic or wound care
Yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, or abdominal pain — suggests liver involvement or hepatic dysfunction; excluded condition
Difficulty breathing, throat swelling, or facial edema — signs of anaphylaxis or severe allergic reaction; emergency care needed
Inability to eat due to oral symptoms (sticky mouth, sores) or severe nausea/vomiting — risk of malnutrition and dehydration
Confusion, dizziness, fainting, or severe fatigue disproportionate to baseline — may indicate electrolyte imbalance or systemic infection
contraindications: Do NOT use warming tonifying herbs (such as Ren Shen ginseng, Lu Rong deer antler, or Rou Gui cinnamon) — these will aggravate Heat and worsen the rash
Do NOT use strong spicy foods or warming spices (chili peppers, black pepper in excess, dried ginger) — heat aggravates the skin condition and increases itching

Do NOT scratch the lesions vigorously — can break the skin barrier, introduce bacterial infection, and spread heat-toxin; if itching is unbearable, apply cool (not cold) wet compress or use the acupoint massage instead
Do NOT take hot baths or use heating pads — external heat will intensify the condition; use warm or cool showers instead
Do NOT use harsh soaps, alcohol-based skin products, or strong essential oils — these irritate skin and aggravate inflammation; use gentle unscented cleanser only
Do NOT wear synthetic fabrics or tight clothing over lesions — use loose, breathable cotton clothing to prevent moisture trapping and maceration
Do NOT stop the herbal treatment abruptly if symptoms improve within 1–2 weeks — premature cessation allows rapid relapse; continue the full 2–3 week course at minimum
precautions.special_notes: This patient's 20-year history means the condition has likely caused secondary changes: possible chronic Liver Blood involvement (emotional stress, itching), possible digestive tract changes (chronic inflammation of intestinal lining from years of damp-heat), and possible Yin deficiency from long-term Heat consumption. Therefore: (1) Initial herbal treatment may cause a temporary worsening of itching or skin inflammation—this is a 'clearing reaction' (排毒反应) and should not alarm; continue for 3–5 more days to confirm improvement. (2) If appetite worsens significantly during treatment, the cold herbs may be over-cooling the Spleen; inform the TCM practitioner to reduce bitter-cold herbs and increase bland tonifying herbs. (3) Monitor stool consistency daily—if stools become very loose, reduce the dose of damp-draining herbs temporarily. (4) Skin lesions may take 4–8 weeks to fully heal; do not expect complete clearing in 2 weeks. (5) Even after skin clears, continue dietary modification and acupoint massage for another 2–3 months to prevent recurrence. (6) Age 68: the underlying Yang Qi is naturally declining; excessive cold herbs or aggressive cooling can cause long-term digestive weakness. The modified formula above is designed to avoid this, but close clinical follow-up is important. (7) This patient is at risk for secondary bacterial infection due to the yellow exudate and crusting; if any fever or systemic symptoms appear, conventional medical evaluation (bacterial culture, sensitivity testing) is appropriate before continuing TCM treatment.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess at 2–3 weeks of consistent herbal treatment. At that visit, evaluate: (1) intensity of itching (reduced or unchanged?), (2) quality and color of skin lesions (exudate cleared? crusts falling off?), (3) sleep quality (improved?), (4) appetite and stool consistency (normalized?), (5) energy and fatigue (improved?). If significant improvement: continue the formula for another 1–2 weeks, then transition to a gentler Spleen-tonifying maintenance formula. If minimal or no improvement: reassess diagnosis (check for secondary infection, allergic component, or systemic condition such as hepatic disease); adjust formula or consider conventional dermatology consultation. If worsening: stop treatment immediately and seek conventional medical evaluation.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1: Itching intensity begins to decrease, sleep disturbance lessens, appetite slightly improves. Week 2–3: Noticeable reduction in redness and swelling, some crust separation and healing of lesions, continued appetite improvement, complete normalization of bowel function. Week 4–8: Majority of active lesions dried and healing, minimal residual redness, full return of appetite and energy, stable sleep. Week 8–12: Complete skin clearance or very minor residual scarring (depending on lesion depth and duration), full constitutional Spleen tonification, zero recurrence over this period.
follow_up.next_steps: After initial 2–3 week intensive clearing phase: (1) Transition to a milder maintenance formula emphasizing Spleen tonification (such as Si Jun Zi Tang or variants with added skin-healing herbs) to prevent recurrence; take for 2–3 additional months. (2) Continue dietary modification indefinitely—this is a constitutional condition and diet is the long-term preventive. (3) Perform acupoint massage maintenance 3–4 times per week rather than daily, to keep Spleen Qi and water metabolism balanced. (4) Consider professional acupuncture treatment (not self-acupressure) if available, 1–2 times per week for 4–8 weeks, to accelerate healing and deepen constitutional change. (5) Reassess emotional wellbeing; if chronic stress or anxiety is identified, add stress management or counseling to prevent relapse. (6) Return for follow-up every 4 weeks for the first 3 months, then every 8 weeks for 6–12 months to monitor for recurrence and adjust formula as Spleen function strengthens. (7) If this chronic condition proves resistant after 12 weeks of consistent treatment, request advanced diagnostics (blood work, possible allergy testing, dermatology specialist evaluation) to exclude underlying systemic disease such as autoimmune dermatitis or hepatic involvement.

parsed.disclaimer: Traditional Chinese Medicine, including herbal therapy and acupoint massage, is a complementary healing system and is NOT a replacement for conventional medical care. This TCM diagnosis and recommendations are intended to support your health and work alongside any medical treatment your doctor prescribes. Before starting any herbal formula, especially if you are taking medications, have other medical conditions, or are over 65 years old, consult with both your TCM practitioner AND your conventional physician to ensure safety and avoid drug-herb interactions. If you experience any of the warning signs listed above, seek immediate conventional medical evaluation. Self-massage and lifestyle modifications have no known serious side effects, but professional acupuncture should only be performed by a licensed acupuncturist. The long-term prognosis of this 20-year chronic condition depends on consistent adherence to herbal treatment, dietary change, and lifestyle modification—improvement will take weeks to months and requires patience. TCM views health as a dynamic process; this assessment reflects your condition at this moment and may need adjustment as your constitution changes during treatment.

data.wen_inquiry: Chief complaint: Twenty years of recurrent scaly red rash over the whole body with severe itching, worse in the last week. Symptoms: sticky feeling in the mouth; poor appetite; fatigue; heavy body sensation; sticky stools with incomplete evacuation; yellowish exudate and crusting on skin; itching disturbing sleep.
